passages.t: Servants and stewards, judged by the Lord
passages.happening:
Paul tells the church how to think of its leaders. “So then, men ought to regard us as servants of Christ and stewards of the mysteries of God” (verse 1). And what matters in a steward is plain: “Now it is required of stewards that they be found faithful” (verse 2).

So Paul does not much mind what the Corinthians think of him. “I care very little, however, if I am judged by you or by any human court. In fact, I do not even judge myself” (verse 3).

He knows of nothing against himself, “but that does not vindicate me. It is the Lord who judges me” (verse 4).

So they should stop passing judgment before the time. “Therefore judge nothing before the appointed time; wait until the Lord comes” (verse 5). He will bring hidden things into the light and show the motives of every heart. “At that time each will receive his praise from God” (verse 5).
passages.hearers:
A steward, in Greek oikonomos, was a household manager. In a large Roman household he was often a trusted slave or freed slave who ran the master's affairs: the money, the stores, the other slaves. He handled what belonged to someone else. The one thing a steward had to be was trustworthy. English gets the word economy from oikonomos.

‘Servants’ here is a different word from the one in 3:5. It is hypēretēs, an assistant who carries out another's orders. Both words say the same thing: Paul and Apollos work under orders. They do not own the church.

The Corinthians had been examining their leaders like judges: comparing their speaking, their learning, their looks. The word Paul uses for ‘judged’ in verse 3 is anakrinō, a word for questioning in a court. Paul says, in effect, ‘You are not my court.’

He goes further. He will not even trust his own verdict on himself. A clear conscience is good, but it is not the final word. People can be blind to their own faults. Only the Lord sees the heart.

Notice how the passage ends. Not with blame, but with praise: ‘each will receive his praise from God’. In a city where people fought for public honour, Paul points to the only praise that will last.
passages.ot:
Paul's confidence that only God truly sees the heart is deep in the Old Testament. When Samuel looked at the tall son of Jesse, God said, “For man sees the outward appearance, but the LORD sees the heart” (1 Samuel 16:7). Through Jeremiah God says, “I, the LORD, search the heart; I examine the mind” (Jeremiah 17:10).

‘He will bring to light what is hidden in darkness’ (verse 5) echoes the end of Ecclesiastes: “For God will bring every deed into judgment, along with every hidden thing, whether good or evil” (Ecclesiastes 12:14). Daniel praises the God who “reveals the deep and hidden things” (Daniel 2:22).

The teaching of Jesus stands behind ‘judge nothing before the appointed time’: “Do not judge, or you will be judged” (Matthew 7:1).
passages.hard:
Does ‘judge nothing’ mean a church can never say that anything is wrong, or that leaders are beyond question?

No. In the very next chapter Paul tells the church it must act in a case of serious sin (5:12). And the steward must be ‘found faithful’, which means his work can be looked at. What Paul forbids here is the Corinthians' habit of ranking and sentencing their teachers, judging motives no one can see, as if the final verdict were theirs.

Nor does ‘I do not even judge myself’ put a leader above being questioned. Paul says the opposite: his own clear conscience does not clear him. Every leader answers to the Lord, and the Lord sees what is hidden. That is a warning to leaders before it is a comfort.
passages.asks: Ask whose verdict on you matters most: other people's, your own, or the Lord's. If you lead in any way, ask whether you are faithful with what is not yours. And if you are quick to sum up other people's motives, Paul's words are a brake: wait. The Lord will show what is in every heart, including yours.

passages.t: ‘What do you have that you did not receive?’
passages.happening:
Paul says why he has written of himself and Apollos. He has used them as an example, “so that you may learn from us not to go beyond what is written. Then you will not take pride in one man over another” (verse 6).

Then three questions. “For who makes you so superior? What do you have that you did not receive? And if you did receive it, why do you boast as though you did not?” (verse 7).
passages.hearers:
‘Do not go beyond what is written’ is a hard phrase, and readers are not sure what it points to. Many think it means the Scriptures Paul has just quoted (1:19, 1:31, 3:19-20), all of which warn against human pride. Others think it was a saying the Corinthians knew, like ‘keep to the rules’. Either way the point is clear: stay humble, and do not puff up one leader against another.

‘Take pride’ translates physioō, to puff up or inflate. It is a favourite word of this letter. Paul uses it six times in 1 Corinthians, and it appears only once more in the whole New Testament (Colossians 2:18). The Corinthians were swollen with pride.

The questions in verse 7 would cut deep in Corinth. The city was full of people who had made themselves: freed slaves who had grown rich, men who had bought or earned office, families who had their gifts cut in stone. Paul asks what anyone has that was not given. Your gifts, your mind, your faith, even your life: all received.

If everything is a gift, boasting makes no sense. You cannot take credit for a present.
passages.ot:
Moses warned Israel against the same pride when they came into the land. They might say to themselves, “The power and strength of my hands have made this wealth for me” (Deuteronomy 8:17). Instead, “remember that it is the LORD your God who gives you the power to gain wealth” (Deuteronomy 8:18).

King David prayed the same truth when the people gave gifts for the temple: “For everything comes from You, and from Your own hand we have given to You” (1 Chronicles 29:14).

And the scriptures Paul has quoted so far, Isaiah 29:14, Jeremiah 9:24, Job 5:13 and Psalm 94:11, all say one thing: God brings down the proud.
passages.asks: Paul's question is one of the most searching in the Bible. Make a list of the things you are proud of: your skills, your knowledge, your family, your faith. Then ask of each one: what do I have that I did not receive? Ask what gratitude would look like where pride has been.

passages.t: Kings in Corinth, and ‘a spectacle to the whole world’
passages.happening:
Now Paul turns to irony. “Already you have all you want. Already you have become rich. Without us, you have become kings” (verse 8). He wishes they really did reign, so that the apostles might reign with them.

Then he sets the apostles beside them. “For it seems to me that God has displayed us apostles at the end of the procession, like prisoners appointed for death. We have become a spectacle to the whole world, to angels as well as to men” (verse 9).

“We are fools for Christ, but you are wise in Christ. We are weak, but you are strong. You are honored, but we are dishonored” (verse 10).

He lists the apostles' life: hungry and thirsty, poorly clothed, beaten, homeless (verse 11). “We work hard with our own hands. When we are vilified, we bless; when we are persecuted, we endure it” (verse 12). When slandered, they answer kindly. “Up to this moment we have become the scum of the earth, the refuse of the world” (verse 13).
passages.hearers:
The Corinthians behaved as if the kingdom had already fully come for them. They were rich in gifts, full of knowledge, sure of their standing. Paul's words in verse 8 are sharp: you have become kings, without us.

The picture in verse 9 comes from Roman public life. Readers see one of two scenes. Some see a Roman triumph, the great parade for a victorious general, with prisoners of war led at the very end, some to be put to death. Others see the arena, where condemned criminals were brought out last, to die before the crowd. Either way, the apostles are the condemned at the end of the show. The whole world, angels and people, are watching.

The three pairs in verse 10 sound like a list of status in Corinth: wise or foolish, strong or weak, honoured or dishonoured. The Corinthians had placed themselves in the top row. The apostles stand in the bottom row, for Christ's sake.

Verse 12 would have startled educated hearers. Hand work was looked down on by the well-to-do, and a teacher was expected to be paid by students or a patron. Paul worked as a tentmaker so as not to be a burden (Acts 18:3; 20:34).

‘Scum’ and ‘refuse’ translate words for what is scraped off or swept away: the dirt from a pot, the sweepings from a floor. People used them of human beings thought worthless. That is how the world saw the apostles.
passages.ot:
The apostles' lives echo the Psalms and the prophets. A psalm says, “Yet for Your sake we face death all day long; we are considered as sheep to be slaughtered” (Psalm 44:22). Paul quotes those words of himself in Romans 8:36. Lamentations mourns, “You have made us scum and refuse among the nations” (Lamentations 3:45).

Above all, the apostles' life follows the Servant of the Lord in Isaiah: “He was despised and rejected by men” (Isaiah 53:3).

The words ‘When we are vilified, we bless’ follow the teaching of Jesus: “bless those who curse you, pray for those who mistreat you” (Luke 6:28). And the homeless apostles follow a Lord who said, “the Son of Man has no place to lay His head” (Matthew 8:20).
passages.asks: The Corinthians thought success meant being rich, wise and honoured. Paul says following Christ may look like the opposite. Ask what you count as the signs of God's blessing on your life. Then ask how you answer people who insult or mistreat you. Paul's ‘we bless’ is not a feeling. It is a choice, and Jesus made it first.

passages.happening:
Paul's tone changes. “I am not writing this to shame you, but to warn you as my beloved children” (verse 14).

“Even if you have ten thousand guardians in Christ, you do not have many fathers; for in Christ Jesus I became your father through the gospel” (verse 15). “Therefore I urge you to imitate me” (verse 16).

That is why he has sent Timothy, “my beloved and faithful child in the Lord” (verse 17). Timothy will remind them of Paul's way of life in Christ, which is what he teaches in every church.

Some have become arrogant, as if Paul were never coming (verse 18). But he will come soon, if the Lord wills, and find out what power these proud people really have (verse 19). “For the kingdom of God is not a matter of talk but of power” (verse 20).

He leaves the choice to them: “Shall I come to you with a rod, or in love and with a gentle spirit?” (verse 21).
passages.hearers:
The ‘guardian’ in verse 15 is the Greek paidagōgos. In a Roman household he was usually a slave who took a boy to school, watched over his behaviour and kept him in line. He was a familiar figure, and not always a loved one. A father was different: his bond with his child was for life.

Paul claims to be their father because he brought them the gospel. Others had taught them since, and may teach them still. But he alone was there at their birth in Christ.

In the ancient world children learned a trade by watching a parent and copying. Students learned from a teacher by living near him. So ‘imitate me’ meant ‘live the way I live’. And the life Paul has just described is hunger, hard work, insults returned with blessing. That is what he asks them to copy.

Timothy had helped found the church in Corinth (2 Corinthians 1:19). He was a younger man, son of a Jewish mother and a Greek father (Acts 16:1). Acts says Paul sent him ahead into Macedonia while Paul stayed in Asia (Acts 19:22).

‘Talk’ and ‘power’ in verse 20 answer the Corinthians' pride in speech. Fine words are cheap. The kingdom of God shows itself in lives changed by God's power, the power of the cross (1:18).
passages.ot:
The picture of God as a father who corrects the children he loves runs through the Old Testament: “for the LORD disciplines the one He loves, as does a father the son in whom he delights” (Proverbs 3:12). Moses told Israel, “just as a man disciplines his son, so the LORD your God disciplines you” (Deuteronomy 8:5).

The ‘rod’ was the common picture for correction and for authority. Proverbs uses it of a parent's discipline (Proverbs 13:24). In the Psalms it can mean a ruler's sceptre (Psalm 2:9). Paul uses it as a picture of a firm, correcting visit.
passages.hard:
Is it arrogant for Paul to say ‘imitate me’? To modern ears it can sound proud. But teachers in Paul's world offered their own lives as a model, and students learned by copying. And look at what Paul asks them to copy: a life of weakness, hard work and blessing those who curse. Later he says what it rests on: “You are to imitate me, just as I imitate Christ” (11:1). Any leader may say it only if what people see in them is the shape of the cross.

What about the ‘rod’? It is a picture of a stern visit, not a word about striking anyone. Paul's own wish is to come ‘in love and with a gentle spirit’, and he puts the choice in their hands. Nothing here gives any parent, pastor or leader leave to hurt a child or anyone in their care.

What if ‘father’ is a hard word for you? Some readers had a father who was absent, or who hurt them. Paul is describing what a father in the faith should be: someone who gives life, warns out of love, and does not shame. If your own father was not that, this is a picture of what you should have been shown. A psalm says, “Though my father and mother forsake me, the LORD will receive me” (Psalm 27:10). If what happened to you still weighs on you, please talk with someone you trust, a pastor, a friend or a counsellor. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
passages.asks: Ask who has been a father or mother in the faith to you, and what in their way of life, not only their words, has shaped yours. Then ask whose life is watching yours, and what they would learn by copying it. Paul's test is whether people see the cross in it.
